read: partial: main text (pages 1-9) and appendices A.1, A.2 and A.5-A.7 in full; appendices A.3-A.4, B, C and E skimmed
what_it_is: A rule-verifiable, process-level benchmark for chemical reasoning: 5,620 samples over 18 reporting tasks (31 fine-grained) in molecular understanding, molecule editing, molecular optimisation and reaction prediction, drawn from public databases and reaction corpora (PubChem, ChEMBL, ZINC, USPTO-derived sets) (p.1, p.3, p.11). Models must answer in expert-refined step templates, induced from natural chain-of-thought by an LLM and pruned by chemists, whose structured fields are scored at three layers reported separately: final-answer correctness, template adherence, and step-wise verifier correctness, the last by deterministic RDKit checks (Type-I), agreement with verified reference traces for closed-answer tasks (Type-II), or property oracles for optimisation (p.2-5). The reference traces are generated by GPT-5.4 and Claude-Opus-4.7 given the ground-truth answer and kept only if they pass the rule checks (p.3, p.9). Eight frontier LLMs are evaluated (p.5, p.7).
domain: chemistry (2D molecular and reaction reasoning), not engineering (p.1, p.9)
size: 5,620 samples, 18 reporting tasks, 31 fine-grained tasks (p.1, p.11); 8 models (p.5, p.7)
source_of_items: public chemistry databases and reaction corpora, standardised with RDKit; molecule-editing instructions written by GPT-5.4 (p.3, p.11, p.19)
instances: static: sampled from databases, with condition-ranking labels shuffled to remove an order shortcut (p.3, p.14)
has_gold_traces: partial: reference traces generated by two LLMs with the ground-truth answer and filtered by rule checks, described by the authors as 'verified benchmark-state trajectories rather than unique human reasoning processes' (p.3, p.9)
evaluation: step-level or process, by deterministic verifiers: L1 task-specific outcome metrics; L2 template-adherence state score; L3 Type-I RDKit all-pass rate, Type-II all-match rate against reference traces, or an oracle score for optimisation (p.4-5); no LLM judge
human_validation: Three expert chemists independently labelled 300 sampled step-level traces as correct, incorrect or ambiguous; the verifier agreed with the majority label on 87.4% of steps (Cohen's kappa 0.74), against human-human agreement of 90.1% (kappa 0.79); disagreements concentrated in tasks with several valid paths (p.14). Chemists also pruned the template fields (p.3).
contamination_measures: none beyond removing answer-leaking metadata and shuffling condition labels (p.3, p.11, p.14)

engtrace_use.explanation: Belongs in: the process supervision and judge validity paragraph, as a deterministic-verifier precedent from a science domain. Candidate, not cited in the May paper. Outside engineering, but its verification design is the closest found to EngTrace's: intermediate states checked deterministically against verified references, outcome and process reported separately, and an expert check of the verifier with agreement statistics (p.4-5, p.14).

suggested_wording: In chemistry, ChemCoTBench-V2 (Guo et al., 2026) has models fill expert-refined step templates and checks the fields with deterministic RDKit rules and rule-filtered reference traces, reporting outcome, template adherence and step validity separately; its verifier agreed with the majority label of three chemists on 87.4% of 300 sampled steps (kappa 0.74).
facts_to_cite: 5,620 samples over 18 reporting tasks (31 fine-grained) in four task families (p.1, p.11)
items drawn from public databases (PubChem, ChEMBL, ZINC, USPTO-derived reactions) and standardised with RDKit (p.3, p.11)
step templates induced from natural chain-of-thought by an LLM and pruned by chemistry experts; models must answer in them (p.3)
reference traces generated by GPT-5.4 and Claude-Opus-4.7 with the ground-truth answer, kept only if they pass the rule checks (p.3, p.9)

three layers reported separately: outcome, template adherence, and step-wise verifier correctness (Type-I RDKit checks, Type-II agreement with reference traces, oracle checks for optimisation) (p.4-5)
for condition ranking, Type-I validity reaches 99.4% but Type-II agreement only 11.6% (p.7)
three expert chemists on 300 sampled steps: verifier-expert agreement 87.4% (kappa 0.74), human-human 90.1% (kappa 0.79) (p.14)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: process-level evaluation by deterministic checks rather than an LLM judge; separate outcome and process scores; references verified by rules; expert validation of the verifier with agreement statistics (p.14). Lacks: an engineering domain and numeric multi-step calculation; generated instances (database samples); gold traces computed by code (references are written by LLMs that were given the answer, p.3, p.9); evaluation of the model's own solution layout (models must fill task-specific template fields, p.3, p.9). What EngTrace adds: instances generated from templates in five engineering branches; gold values computed by the template code; milestones matched anywhere in a generic numbered-step solution, plus per-claim arithmetic checks, rather than task-specific fields; and a residual LLM judge, validated against experts, for what the deterministic checks miss.
notes: (1) Outside engineering, so it is not a must for the engineering paragraph; I rate it should because its deterministic step verification and its verifier-expert kappa are the nearest analogue to EngTrace's evaluator evidence. (2) The arXiv file is v2 (3 June 2026); the catalogue date (2026-06) agrees. (3) The search note says reference traces are checked 'instead of an LLM judge', which holds for scoring; the references themselves are LLM-generated given the answer (p.3), so the gold traces are not code-derived. (4) Code is linked at github.com/fresnellll/ChemCoTBench-V2 (p.1).
